system_description.narrative_title: Strategic Fragmentation: Energy Shocks, Power Rivalry, Market Volatility
system_description.narrative_summary: The international order is an open, tightly coupled system in which a Middle East standoff over the Strait of Hormuz, persistent Russia–Ukraine combat, and accelerating great‑power competition (economic, military and technological) interact to drive global energy, financial and supply‑chain shocks. Markets and central banks are reacting to this security‑market feedback loop—currency interventions, volatile bond yields and oil spikes—while states form ad‑hoc defence pacts and pursue alternative trade and shipping corridors. These dynamics amplify each other: disruptions in one domain (e.g., Hormuz closure or drone strikes) cascade into commodity, inflation and liquidity stresses that reshape alliance choices and industrial policy.
system_description.scope: State-level security conflicts and alliances, regional crises (Middle East, Europe–Russia, Indo‑Pacific), global commodity and energy flows, international financial and monetary dynamics (FX, bond markets, central bank policy), technology competition and supply chains (AI, semiconductors, Arctic shipping), and cross-border migration and humanitarian pressures.
system_description.super_system: The global political‑economic system: the international order of states, markets, institutions and transnational actors that governs security, trade, finance and technology interactions.
adjacent_subsystems: Global energy and commodity markets (oil, shipping chokepoints, refineries)
International financial and monetary system (FX markets, central banks, sovereign balance sheets)
Technology and high‑value supply chains (AI infrastructure, semiconductors, Arctic shipping routes)

variables.name: Strait of Hormuz standoff
variables.description: Iran, the United States and Gulf states (with Houthi and proxy actions) are locked in a bargaining and coercion conflict over control of the Hormuz maritime chokepoint that is driving sustained oil-supply disruption and regional security realignment.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine high‑intensity war
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine, backed respectively by different external patrons and arms flows, are engaged in an attritional, escalating campaign (including long‑range strikes, drones and naval/Black Sea operations) that is reshaping battlefield dynamics, weapons demand and European security posture.

variables.name: US–China tech and industrial rivalry
variables.description: The United States and China, together with allied firms and third‑country suppliers, are competing for dominance in semiconductors, AI, shipbuilding and critical supply chains through export controls, industrial policy and financing that are shifting global technological leadership and economic interdependence.

variables.name: Taiwan cross‑strait militarization
variables.description: China and Taiwan, with the United States and regional partners conducting exercises and deterrence measures, are experiencing rising military activity, drills and preparations that increase the risk of rapid escalation across the first island chain.

variables.name: Global currency and monetary frictions
variables.description: Major central banks and states (notably the US and Japan) are intervening and signalling divergent policy paths amid shifting inflation and debt dynamics, creating new currency activism, coordination pressures and strains on international capital flows and reserve management.
